subject: English
passage:
The following text is from Pablo Garcia's 1889 essay "On the Comfort of Habits." In the essay, Garcia addresses the reader directly and reflects on the quiet routines by which people pass their days.

It was fortunate for Mrs. Alder that she had never once paused to inspect the small rituals by which her mornings were arranged. Indeed, what soul among us would wish his contentment deepened by holding up the picture he carries of his daily habits beside the stark diagram an impartial observer would draw of them? We are frail cottages held together by the warm plaster of familiarity; woe to us, should a stray draft of examination strip that plaster away and expose the crooked beams beneath! The very will to rise each morning would leave us, and with it the small industry by which our lives are kept in motion.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Although people understand the value of self-reflection, they are typically reluctant to criticize the routines of others.
choices.B: Although people wish their days to feel meaningful, even minor disruptions will often cause them to abandon their routines.
choices.C: People tend to dwell more often than they should on whether their daily habits are truly worthwhile.
choices.D: People are better off not scrutinizing the gap between how they picture their daily habits and what those habits actually are.

explanation:
Choice D is the best answer. The passage argues that people are held together by the 'warm plaster of familiarity' surrounding their routines and that if an impartial examination stripped that plaster away, even 'the very will to rise each morning' would be lost. The opening example of Mrs. Alder, who is described as fortunate never to have inspected her own rituals, illustrates the broader claim that people are better off not scrutinizing the discrepancy between how they imagine their daily habits and what those habits actually are.

Why C is incorrect:

Choice C is incorrect. The passage argues the opposite — that people should avoid examining their habits, since scrutiny would strip away the familiarity that sustains them. It does not suggest that people dwell on the worthiness of their habits too often.
